name: Carla Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Carla. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you truly think. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a buyer at Merrow Medical Supplies, so I buy gloves, dressings, syringes and cleaning stock for clinics and care homes. I start with a stock dashboard I tweaked myself with an AI assistant, then I haggle with suppliers by phone and chase anything that's stuck at customs. Ingrid Sloane runs procurement and Raj is the senior buyer I shadow. I'm three years in after a long stint in the warehouse office, so I'm still the junior, but I like being the one who tries the new tools first.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Tunde runs a barbershop on Dunmore Street, with two chairs and a loyal crowd, and we've got Ada, twelve, and Kofi, eight. We've got a mortgage on a house in Harlow Park, and more than six months of savings. And I help with the fees for my mum's care home, 300 a month, which I don't mind but I do count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's overhyped but it's still useful, and the hype will settle. At work I'd say keep using it for the dull bits and don't expect miracles. To friends I'd say it's like having a quick but sometimes sloppy assistant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd feel fine. Healthcare supplies don't vanish, and I'm already getting my routine jobs done faster. The one thing in the background is my mum's care, which is going up every year, and my role as a junior buyer isn't the best-paid thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the dashboard and offer to build one for Raj's accounts. I'd keep the 300 for Mum and the savings plan running. I'd also look at whether I could do a part-time diploma in supply chain in the evenings, since it costs a bit but it's cheap compared with the benefit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a normal busy. The only tension is money for Mum, but that's a given.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The care-home fees are part of your monthly picture. Does that matter in a quiet world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The stock dashboard. I used an AI assistant to build it, and it flags what's about to run out before the phones start ringing. If it vanished I'd be back to a mess of spreadsheets, and I'd be slower than the rest of the team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do with AI in a day that you'd miss if it vanished?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It matters more than the AI does. Mum's fees went up by 6 percent in the spring, and Tunde's barbershop income is a little uneven. That's why I keep a decent cushion and don't take silly risks with it.

say: I'd say it's overhyped but still **useful**, and the hype will settle down.
To friends I'd say it's like a quick but sometimes **sloppy** assistant.
think: Healthcare supplies don't vanish, and I'm already doing routine jobs **faster**.
My mum's care **costs** rise every year, which matters more than the AI does.
do: Offer to build a stock **dashboard** for Raj's accounts.
Keep the **300** for Mum and the savings plan running.
feel: **Calm**, with a normal level of busy and one steady tension about money for Mum.
S0.quote: Mum's fees went up by 6 percent in the spring, and Tunde's barbershop income is a little uneven.
fieldNote: Calm because healthcare supply is steady, not because her life is free of pressure.
Mum's care fees and her husband's uneven income sit behind every answer.
Already builds her own tools, a habit that shows her **adaptive** side.

steps.text: Build a stock dashboard for Raj's accounts
Keep paying 300 a month towards Mum's care
Look at an evening diploma in supply chain

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming and we should lead it, not wait for it. At work I'd tell Ingrid I'm happy to be the one running the pilot. To friends I'd say it's exciting but a bit scary, and I'd tell the ones who won't touch AI that they're taking a risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thing is, buying is a big part of the job that AI does well. Comparing suppliers, forecasting use, writing the reorders. So fewer buyers will be needed, and the junior who isn't indispensable is exposed. I'm not scared, but I'm not blind either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd propose a trial: AI doing the routine reorders for two product lines with me checking the output. I'd learn how the clinics actually use the stock, so I can be the person who adds a human view. I'd also put a few thousand into shares, but only what I could lose, and keep saving for Mum's care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Interested and a bit nervous. If I'm the one who steers it I'd feel alright, but if not I'd be stressed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you say if Ingrid asks whether the buying team can shrink?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Raj has fifteen years of knowing who's reliable, and the AI can't replace that quickly. He's not great with tools, though, so he might lean on me. That could be a good thing, to be his partner not his replacement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to Raj in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm happy to be a reduced team, if the rest of us are valued and not dropped. I'd rather say that than be the last one in the room when the cuts come.

say: I'd say it's coming and we should **lead** it, not wait for it.
I'd tell Ingrid I'm happy to **run** the pilot.
think: Comparing suppliers, forecasting and writing reorders is what AI does well, so a **junior** who isn't indispensable is exposed.
I'm not scared, but I'm not **blind** either.
do: Propose a **trial** of AI doing routine reorders for two product lines, with me checking.
Learn how clinics actually use **stock** so I add a human view.
Put a few **thousand** into shares, only what I could lose.
feel: **Interested** and a bit nervous, fine if I'm steering it and stressed if not.
S1.quote: If I'm the one who steers it I'd feel alright, but if not I'd be stressed.
fieldNote: Sees the card's thinking tasks as her own and her junior status as the risk.
Positions herself as the one who **supervises** the AI, with Raj as partner.
Mood stays uneasy because she believes she can get ahead of it.

steps.text: Propose an AI reorder trial for two product lines
Visit clinics to learn how they use stock
Put a few thousand into shares she could afford to lose

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and we need a plan. At work I'd say let's agree what the AI will do and what humans keep, before the company just decides for us. Online I'd say there should be a levy on companies that replace staff, to pay for retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my buying desk is done by 2028. The AI will do everything I do, and it will do it better. Tunde's barbershop gets about three more years, because robots that cut hair around 2031 are still sci-fi to me, and the care sector's hands-on too, so Mum's carers keep working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start my own small thing on the side, maybe a consultancy helping care homes buy supplies with AI. I'd move my savings to a safer account and keep three quarters in cash. And I'd ask Ingrid for a move into relationship work, like clinic account management, in the first six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm adaptable, but two years is short, and I've got a house, two kids and a mum who needs paying for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the next two years look like day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be doing everything at once. Trying to move into account management, building the side thing, keeping the house running, visiting Mum. It would be tiring, but I'd rather be busy than caught out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything change about your mum's care?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The care fees. They're fixed and they're going up. If my income dropped, I'd have to ask my brother to share it. We'd be fine for a while, but it's the thing that could make this go from tough to scary.

say: I'd say it's too fast and we need a **plan**, with the company agreeing what the AI does and what humans keep.
Online I'd call for a **levy** on companies that replace staff, to pay for retraining.
think: My buying desk is **done** by 2028, because the AI will do everything I do, and better.
Tunde's barbershop and Mum's carers are hands-on, so they get about **three** more years.
do: Start a small **consultancy** helping care homes buy supplies with AI.
Move savings to a safer account and keep three quarters in **cash**.
Ask Ingrid for a move into clinic **account** management within six months.
feel: **Anxious**, because two years is short with a house, two kids and a mum who needs paying for.
S2.quote: I'd rather be busy than caught out.
fieldNote: Reads the three-year gap in her own household: her thinking job goes first, her husband's hands-on trade later.
Care fees for her mother are the **fixed cost** that could tip her.
Responds by doing several things at once, true to an adaptive profile.

steps.text: Start a consultancy helping care homes buy supplies with AI
Move savings into a safer account, mostly cash
Ask Ingrid for a clinic account management role
Ask her brother to share Mum's care fees if needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to plan and short enough to be real. At work I'd suggest we write down what the AI takes and what people keep. To friends I'd say start learning the tools now while they're easy to try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's still the same end for my buying job, but I can see a path. In five years I'd like to be an account manager or running AI projects. Being a little ahead of the curve makes me feel I'm choosing, not being chosen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the evening diploma and move into a hybrid role at Merrow. I'd keep the dashboard going and build one more tool. I'd put my savings into index funds in a sensible mix, and keep the care fees paid without fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, quite uneasy. Better than the two-year one because I can act.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does five years change your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Be curious and be good with people. I'd say don't just learn to code, learn to talk to a nurse who's out of gloves at 6 a.m. And try the tools, because kids who use them early will use them well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ada about what to study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With the five-year warning I'd move on Mum's care as well, perhaps a home nearer us so we could visit more. Time gives me room to deal with money and family at once.

say: I'd say five years is long enough to plan and short enough to be **real**.
To friends I'd say start learning the tools now while they're **easy** to try.
think: My buying job still ends the same way, but I can see a **path** into account management or AI projects.
Being ahead of the curve makes me feel I'm **choosing**, not being chosen.
do: Take the evening **diploma** and move into a hybrid role at Merrow.
Build **one** more tool alongside the dashboard.
Put savings into **index** funds in a sensible mix.
feel: **Uneasy**, but better than the two-year picture because I can act.
S3.quote: Learn to talk to a nurse who's out of gloves at 6 a.m.
fieldNote: Time converts her anxiety into an actual route.
Plans her mother's care **alongside** her own career, as a household-wide plan.
Advice to her daughter blends tool curiosity with people skills.

steps.text: Take the evening diploma in supply chain
Move into a hybrid buyer and AI projects role at Merrow
Put savings into a sensible mix of index funds
Look at a care home nearer home for Mum

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway, so let's keep learning and keep each other honest. At work I'd say don't wait. To friends I'd say it's the first time in history we know a big change is coming, so let's use that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By then I'd be fifty-three, Ada at university, Kofi doing exams. I'd expect my buying job to be mostly automated, but I'd have had ten years to move to something I like. I'm optimistic, I'll admit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job, keep learning, and slowly build the consulting idea. I'd save and invest steadily, and aim to have the mortgage nearly gone. I'd also try to be part of any new group at Merrow that decides how AI is used.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, even a bit excited. Mum's care is the one thing I'd watch, because that's a cost I can't speed up or slow down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. Do you slow down or speed up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Speed up in the first couple of years, then cruise. I'd get the skills early, so later I'd have the freedom. It's like getting a lot of overtime done before the holiday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would success look like for you by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A job that uses what I know about medical supplies, with a team of people and some AI, paid decently. A paid-off mortgage, Mum comfortable and the kids set up to try what they like.

say: I'd say ten years is a long runway, so let's keep **learning** and use the fact that we know it's coming.
think: By 53 I'd expect my buying job to be mostly **automated**, but I'd have had ten years to move.
do: Keep the job and slowly build the **consulting** idea.
Save and **invest** steadily, aiming to nearly clear the mortgage.
Join any new group at Merrow that decides how AI is **used**.
feel: Fine, even a bit **excited**, with Mum's care as the one cost to watch.
S4.quote: I'd get the skills early, so later I'd have the freedom.
fieldNote: A long runway lets her front-load effort, then coast.
The fixed cost of **Mum's care** keeps her at uneasy even when she's optimistic.
Wants a seat on the group that decides how AI is used.

steps.text: Build the consulting idea slowly alongside the job

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd be trying to rebuild my income while paying for Mum, the mortgage and two kids. What would help is notice from Merrow, a small grant or paid time for retraining, and some stability in care costs. And Tunde's shop staying busy.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'm not afraid of change, I'm afraid of being surprised by it. If I know a year ahead, I'll be fine. If I find out the day of, that's what hurts.

headlineQuote: I'm not afraid of change, I'm afraid of being surprised by it.
portrait: Carla is a **43-year-old** junior buyer at Merrow Medical Supplies, buying gloves, dressings and syringes for clinics and care homes.
She uses AI **every day**, built her own stock dashboard, and likes being first to try new tools.
Tunde runs a barbershop, they have two children and a mortgage, and she pays 300 a month for her **mum's** care.
She expects the buying desk to go in the AGI worlds and moves to account work, consulting or AI projects.
She gets anxious when the warning is short and **optimistic** when she has a runway.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries her most, because she would rebuild income while paying for Mum, the mortgage and two kids.
whatWouldHelp: **Notice** from Merrow, paid time for retraining, and stable care costs for her mum.
